Changing a C# field does not automatically tell the screen. Notifications are the message saying “this property changed; please redraw it.”

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

INotifyPropertyChanged

public event PropertyChangedEventHandler? PropertyChanged;
void Changed([CallerMemberName] string? property = null) =>
    PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(property));

The property setter updates its backing field and raises the event with the property name. CallerMemberName avoids repeatedly typing the name. A wrong name can stop the expected UI refresh. ObservableCollection handles collection changes, but an item’s changing properties still need their own notifications.

Validate without crashing

The sample implements IDataErrorInfo. Its indexer returns a message for Name or AgeText. XAML sets ValidatesOnDataErrors=True. AgeText is a string so incomplete typing does not cause repeated conversion exceptions; int.TryParse checks it. Red validation feedback and a disabled command guide the user. Server-side validation is still required if the ViewModel later calls an API.

Expected checks

Blank name: invalid. Name over 80 characters: invalid. Age abc,15 or101: invalid. A normal name and age22 enable Add. After Add, the list changes and inputs reset. A larger app can use INotifyDataErrorInfo for asynchronous validation.

Try it yourself

Why does changing a field directly not refresh a bound TextBlock?

Worked answer

No PropertyChanged notification was raised. Set through a notifying property.

Does desktop validation replace API validation?

Worked answer

No. Any client can send requests. The server independently enforces its rules.
